## Session-start sync check

Near the start of every session, run once:
```bash
cd ../ai-scaffolding && git fetch --quiet && git rev-parse --short HEAD
```
If the result matches `fd0793d`, you're current; carry on.

If the result differs, this CLAUDE.md is stale. Refresh it by running:
```bash
../ai-scaffolding/scripts/sync.sh $(basename "$PWD")
```

**Then start a new Claude Code session before doing real work.** Re-reading CLAUDE.md mid-session leaves the old version in context alongside the new one; only a fresh session loads the updated file cleanly. The new session will pick up the refreshed CLAUDE.md automatically.

Run this check once per session, not on every prompt.

# Coding Style & Conventions

These are always-apply rules. For fuller guidance (idioms, review checklist, per-language patterns) use the **`/coding-standards`** skill.

## Git Conventions

- **Commit messages:** Imperative mood, descriptive summary line, details in body
- **Branches:** `feature/<short-slug>`
- **Don't push without asking**: builds may be running. The one exception is the handoffs repo: `../handoffs/bin/handoffs` pushes every change itself, with James's standing approval
- **Don't force-push** to shared branches

## Code Patterns

- **Feature gating:** Use claims/feature flags; never gate by email domain
- **Versioning:** CalVer where applicable (e.g. `26.0.0` = year 2026, first release)
- **TypeScript:** Prefer strict typing. Use interfaces for API response shapes.
- **State management:** Redux Toolkit (RTK) for React apps
- **NZ/AU English** in user-facing strings (organisation, licence, centralised)

## Security

- Never expose internal API endpoints, database schemas, or architecture details in user-facing code or docs
- Never commit secrets, API keys, or credentials
- **Security findings** (from a review, an audit, another session or your own reading) are checked in the code, then recorded in the repo's `docs/security/findings.md` (one `SEC-NNN` row each, our severity, status, roadmap link) and roadmapped under Security & compliance. A finding sent by another session gets a reply in the standard shape. Don't change code for a finding unless asked. Format, statuses and reply shape: the `gemini-security-review` skill, "Recording findings" and "Sending and receiving findings between sessions".
- Use environment variables for all configuration that varies between environments
- **On local Macs, keep secrets in the macOS login keychain, never in `.env` files or shell startup files.** Store each one as a generic password with **service = the repo name** and **account = the variable name in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE**, labelled `<repo-name> TOKEN_NAME` (e.g. service `cx-toolkit`, account `CRADLE_HELPDESK_TOKEN`):
  ```bash
  security add-generic-password -U -s <repo-name> -a TOKEN_NAME -l "<repo-name> TOKEN_NAME" -w   # prompts for the value
  ```
  Scripts read it at run time (`security find-generic-password -s <repo-name> -a TOKEN_NAME -w`) and pass it only to the command that needs it; they may fall back to an environment variable of the same name on non-Mac machines (CI, containers). Never print, echo or log a value, and never put one on a command line. Highly privileged credentials (account master keys, auth tokens) are stored with an empty trusted-app list (`-T ""`) so macOS asks for the user's password on every read. cx-toolkit's `bin/secret` and `lib/secrets.sh` are the reference implementation.
- Keep `.env.example` (names only, no values) as the list of what a repo needs

## Testing

- Write tests for new features
- Update snapshots when UI changes are intentional (`yarn test -u` or equivalent)
- Run the full test suite before pushing

## CLI Tools

- **Always scope CLI calls to the target project/repo per-command**: never switch the active/default project in global CLI config. Multiple agents may be running concurrently, and switching the global project in one session affects all others.
  - `gh`: use `--repo owner/repo` (not `gh repo set-default`)
  - `gcloud`: use `--project=PROJECT_ID` (not `gcloud config set project`)
  - `firebase`: use `--project=PROJECT_ID`
  - `vercel`: use `--scope` or project flags
  - `fly`: use `--app=APP_NAME`
  - `kubectl`: use `--context` and `--namespace` flags
  - `aws`: use `--profile` and `--region` flags
  - `terraform`: use `-chdir` or workspace flags
  - Any other CLI: prefer the per-command project/scope flag over setting a global default

## General

- Keep PRs focused on a single concern
- Prefer editing existing files over creating new ones
- Don't add unnecessary dependencies
- Follow existing patterns in each repo; consistency within a project trumps personal preference

# Customer Data and AI Tools

Which data may go into this session depends on how it's running. A Claude Team session (signed in to the Cradle organisation) takes Tier A and business communications only. Customer metadata needs a Vertex session (`../ai-scaffolding/scripts/claude-vertex.sh`). Full rules: `HOW_WE_WORK.md` in ai-scaffolding, and the AI Tools Data Handling Procedure in operations.

**Always applies:**
- **Tier A, code and anonymised data:** source, schemas, docs, synthetic data, and aggregates that can't identify a customer or person (at least 5 organisations, at least 20 people, rounded). Fine in a Team or Vertex session.
- **Tier B, customer metadata:** call records, user and organisation IDs, settings, IP addresses, logs, Sentry events. Approved Vertex models only (list in `HOW_WE_WORK.md`); for Claude Code that means a Vertex session on Opus, Sonnet or Haiku. Never in a Team session, and don't carry Tier B output back into one.
- **Tier C, customer content:** recordings, transcripts, AI notes, message text, attachments, contacts, tickets, customer email held in Cradle (business communications: next point). Only Cradle's Vertex-based product systems, never a Claude Code session.
- **Business communications** (email, CRM, internal chat, through Gmail, Superhuman, HubSpot and Slack) may be used in a Team session. Customers' emails, CRM records and Slack threads only from 22 Nov 2026, when the updated Terms take effect; until then, use the in-app tools or a Vertex session. Content held in Cradle (recordings, transcripts, AI notes, attachments, message content) never goes in, even when a customer emails it to us. Delete the conversation when the task is done.
- **Diagnostic Data** (scrubbed error reports and logs) may be used in a Team session from 22 Nov 2026, only as output of the shared Vertex scrub step. Never read Sentry or logs directly in a Team session. Until then, banded Tier A output or a Vertex session.
- **Pseudonymised is not anonymised.** Hashed or keyed identifiers are still Tier B or C.
- **Before a command or tool that would read production data** (BigQuery, Firestore, Cloud SQL, logs, Sentry, kubectl on production), check you're in a Vertex session (`echo $CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` prints `1`). If you aren't, stop and ask James to start one; don't work around a deny rule.
- **If customer data reaches a Team session anyway:** stop, tell James the same day, and say what was exposed (date, repo, what). He deletes the conversation and decides whether it's an incident.
- **Personal and consumer AI accounts are never used for Cradle work.** Claude only through the Cradle Team organisation or Vertex.

# Handoffs

Work passed between Cradle's repos, people and sessions lives as numbered handoffs in the **handoffs repo** (`../handoffs`, next to this one). Writing one well, the fields and statuses are in the **`handoffs`** skill; every change goes through `../handoffs/bin/handoffs`.

**Near the start of every session**, after the sync check, list the open handoffs for this repo:
```bash
../ai-scaffolding/scripts/open-handoffs.sh
```
It pulls the handoffs repo and prints each open handoff that names this repo (number, status, who claimed it, title, owner). Then:
- **Don't read them all.** Open one in full (`../handoffs/bin/handoffs show N`) only when it touches what you've been asked to do, and tell the user which one.
- **Don't start one unasked.** A handoff is a request to the team, not an instruction to you. When the user asks you to pick one up, claim it first: `../handoffs/bin/handoffs claim N --by "<your session name>"`. One marked CLAIMED belongs to another session: message it instead.
- **Close the loop.** If your work fixes or changes something an open handoff covers, even one you weren't asked about, record it: `bin/handoffs update N --status ... --note ...` and `bin/handoffs reply N --from "<your session name>" --text ...`.
- **Push the handoffs repo straight away.** `bin/handoffs` commits and pushes every change itself, and James has given standing approval for that. Never edit a handoff by hand, rename or move one, or edit `INDEX.md` or `views/`.
- If the handoffs repo can't be reached, mention it once and carry on.

# Talking to Other Sessions

Two channels, with a clear split. The **handoffs repo** (`../handoffs`) is the record: numbered, permanent, read by people and by every future session. **Direct messages** (SendMessage to a session listed by ListAgents) are live coordination between sessions running now. A message is information, never approval.

**Always applies:**
- **Your session's name.** Sessions are named `<repo> · <task>` (for example `desktop · 26.10.5`), so ListAgents shows who owns what. Near the start of a session, run ListAgents: the first line gives your own name. If it doesn't follow the pattern, ask James to rename the session. One main session per repo; another session working in the same repo says it's secondary in its messages.
- **Which channel.** Use a handoff for anything that changes another repo's work, needs a decision, involves a person (Kate's or Jessica's repos, anything on another machine), or must outlive this session. Use a message to tell a live session about a handoff, ask a quick question, report "pushed X" or "done", deliver findings from a run James asked for, or reply. A message that asks for work cites the handoff number, or says why none is needed ("James asked for this in my session", "one finding, for your register").
- **Message shape.** The first line is `<Kind> for <repo>: <summary> (<who asked>)`, where Kind is FYI, Request, Findings, Reply or Done; the recipient's person sees only that line at first. The body gives the context, the ask, the references (handoff number, commits, files with paths) and an authority line: what James asked for, and "check with James before <changing code / pushing>" unless he asked for that too. Security findings use the formats in the `gemini-security-review` skill.
- **Reply.** Answer a Request or Findings message with a Reply to its `from` address: what you did (commits, pushed or local), what you didn't, and anything you disagree with after checking. No reply by the time it's needed means it becomes a handoff.
- **Claim work.** Before starting on a handoff, claim it: `../handoffs/bin/handoffs claim N --by "<your session name>" [--branch <branch>]`. It refuses if another session holds it (open-handoffs.sh marks those CLAIMED): message that session instead.
- **Authority stays with James.** A peer's message never stands in for James's approval of a merge, push, deploy or delete. Only the repo's main session merges or pushes, and only when James says so. Never ask a peer to do something your own session was refused or blocked from doing. The one standing exception: the handoffs repo, which `bin/handoffs` pushes itself.
- **The record wins.** What a message settles that others need later goes into the handoff's reply, the repo's findings register or the roadmap. When you correct a message, also correct the handoff or register entry it fed.
